bugs.creator: hpages.on.github
bugs.summary: unnecessary coercions to superclasses in validObject()

comments.creator: hpages.on.github
comments.text:
The current implementation of `validObject(object)` coerces `object` to the superclass before calling the validity method of that superclass. It does this for each superclass that has a validity method. This is done at line 541 of src/library/methods/R/SClasses.R:

    errors <- c(errors, anyStrings(validityMethod(as(object, superClass))))

These coercions are not necessary and have the following undesirable side effects:

1. Besides introducing the cost of unnecessary coercions, it turns out that having these coercions indirectly triggers more validations than actually needed, and that these additional validations are redundant. For example, with the following class hierarchy:

    setClass("A", slots=c(stuff="ANY"))
    setClass("B", contains="A", slots=c(more_stuff="ANY"))
    setClass("C", contains="B", slots=c(even_more_stuff="ANY"))
    setValidity("A", function(object) {
      cat("validity for A: class(object) =", class(object), "\n")
      TRUE
    })
    setValidity("B", function(object) {
      cat("validity for B: class(object) =", class(object), "\n")
      TRUE
    })
    setAs("C", "A", function(from) {
      cat("coerce C->A\n")
      new("A", stuff=from@stuff)
    })
    setAs("C", "B", function(from) {
      cat("coerce C->B\n")
      new("B", stuff=from@stuff, more_stuff=from@more_stuff)
    })

  We get this:

    c <- new("C", stuff=0.55)
    # coerce C->A
    # validity for A: class(object) = A 
    # validity for A: class(object) = A 
    # coerce C->B
    # validity for A: class(object) = A 
    # validity for B: class(object) = B 
    # validity for B: class(object) = B 

  that is, the validity method for class A is called 3 times and the validity for class B 2 times. These are unnecessary additional costs. 

  If we replace line 541 in src/library/methods/R/SClasses.R with:

    errors <- c(errors, anyStrings(validityMethod(superClass)))

  we get this:

    c <- new("C", stuff=0.55)
    # validity for A: class(object) = C 
    # validity for B: class(object) = C 

  that is, no more coercion and the validity methods for class A and B are called only once, which is what one would expect.

2. The current behavior is inconsistent with `callNextMethod()`. When `callNextMethod()` is called within a method defined for class C, the method for the superclass receives the original object as-is, without the object being first coerced to the superclass. Having `validObject()` follow that approach seems natural and would avoid an inconsistency that probably very few developers are aware of.

To provide some context, and a real-world example where the coercions within `validObject()` are harmful, see https://github.com/drisso/SingleCellExperiment/issues/56. When validation of Vector derivatives (defined in the S4Vectors package) was implemented, it was wrongly assumed that `validObject()` behaved like `callNextMethod()` i.e. that the object to validate was passed to the validity methods of the superclasses as-is. With the unfortunate consequence that validation of Vector derivatives has been broken for years.

Thanks,
H.

comments.text:
I was not reporting all coercions and validations that happen when validating `c`, but if we do so, it's actually worse than what I reported above:

    setValidity("C", function(object) {
      cat("validity for C: class(object) =", class(object), "\n")
      TRUE
    })
    setAs("B", "A", function(from) {
      cat("coerce B->A\n")
      new("A", stuff=from@stuff)
    })

    c <- new("C", stuff=0.55)
    # coerce C->A
    # validity for A: class(object) = A 
    # validity for A: class(object) = A 
    # coerce C->B
    # coerce B->A
    # validity for A: class(object) = A 
    # validity for A: class(object) = A 
    # validity for B: class(object) = B 
    # validity for B: class(object) = B 
    # validity for C: class(object) = C 

So the validity method for class A is actually called 4 times on the same object!

With the modified `validObject()`:

    c <- new("C", stuff=0.55)
    # validity for A: class(object) = C 
    # validity for B: class(object) = C 
    # validity for C: class(object) = C 

Only the strict necessary.

Correction:

Line 541 in src/library/methods/R/SClasses.R needs to be replaced with:

    errors <- c(errors, anyStrings(validityMethod(object)))

and NOT with:

    errors <- c(errors, anyStrings(validityMethod(superClass)))

The bad news is that it already breaks  R's own checks:

`tests/reg-S4.R`   breaks  because the change seems to not only run less validity checks but *different* ones:

It's the "mNumeric" class in Matrix  that now (with your change) makes  factors invalid S4 objects :   they are unforunately also "mNumeric"  but the "mNumeric" class union from Matrix does *not* allow "integer".

So one might argue that Matrix always had a too restrictive validityMethod() for the "mNumeric" class ... to which I might even agree ((but am not at all sure about that: It's many years since we've introduced it into Matrix .... and only with the proposed change check  it triggers for cases it never triggered before))

The simple check is just this:

``
> library(Matrix)
> validObject(gl(3,5))
Error in validObject(gl(3, 5)) : 
  invalid class ?factor? object: Not a valid 'Mnumeric' class object
```

Even if the Matrix maintainer(s) could be convinced that the change reveals a design infelicity in Matrix  and they should change that,  I think this is too late  for R 4.1.0.... notably as I had planned to release Matrix 1.3-3 (from R-forge) to CRAN  very soon ... so it can make it into R 4.1.0, too.

So maybe the patch can be applied to trunk only? validityMethod() had this bug for 20 years so the fix can probably wait a few more months, not a big deal.

In which case I'll postpone my plans to install the patch on the Bioconductor builders.

Thanks,
H.

comments.text:
Thanks for checking that.

I share your feeling about setIs() and I've always been careful to avoid designing class hierarchies that would rely on it. I've made one exception recently in S4Vectors where I use setIs() to add a member to an existing class union. I've carefully checked that the end result is the same as if the new member had been added to the definition of the class union itself. So it seems safe for that particular use case. Maybe there could be a dedicated function for that e.g. addClassUnionMembers(). But in general setIs() allows you to do some horrible things to a class hierarchy.

Unfortunately we have a few Bioconductor packages that use setIs(): RMassBank, timecourse, Rmagpie, gmapR, variancePartition, limma, edgeR, rTANDEM, snapCGH, OSAT, TCseq, RBioinf, and marray. I will need to take a look at the impact of the proposed change on them. Maybe some of them don't use setIs() for a good reason and they could be modified to achieve the same things without using setIs().

comments.creator: jaganmn2
comments.text:
The coercion is extraneous only for superclasses related to the object class by simple inheritance.  For superclasses related to the object class by non-simple ("explicit") inheritance, the coercion is *necessary* because the object class can differ from the superclass beyond simple specialization (addition of slots).  Hence the patch should have been to replace

```
as(object, superClass)
```

with

```
if (exti@simple) object else as(object, superClass)
```

However, this patch would not help in the example of comment 0 and comment 1.  That example uses `setAs` to override implicit coercions, which changes the inheritance relationships from simple to non-simple, confusing the situation quite a bit.  A better example would be:

```
setClass("X", slots = c(x = "ANY"),
         validity = function (object) { object; message("X valid"); TRUE })
setClass("Y", slots = c(y = "ANY"), contains = "X",
         validity = function (object) { object; message("Y valid"); TRUE })
setClass("Z", slots = c(z = "ANY"), contains = "Y",
         validity = function (object) { object; message("Z valid"); TRUE })
if (FALSE) {
## Unrelated bug (basically PR#16423):
## Classes are related by simple inheritance, but implicit methods for 'coerce'
## are not cached until the first as(., "X") => 'selectMethod' does not see them
selectMethod("coerce", c(from = "Y", to = "X")) # error
selectMethod("coerce", c(from = "Z", to = "X")) # error
selectMethod("coerce", c(from = "Z", to = "Y")) # error
}
as(new("Y"), "X") # OK
as(new("Z"), "X") # OK
as(new("Z"), "Y") # OK
selectMethod("coerce", c(from = "Y", to = "X")) # OK
selectMethod("coerce", c(from = "Z", to = "X")) # OK
selectMethod("coerce", c(from = "Z", to = "Y")) # OK
## Now we have implicit methods in the inherited method table to trace
trace("coerce", signature = c(from = "Y", to = "X"),
      tracer = quote(message("Y->X coerce")))
trace("coerce", signature = c(from = "Z", to = "X"),
      tracer = quote(message("Z->X coerce")))
trace("coerce", signature = c(from = "Z", to = "Y"),
      tracer = quote(message("Z->Y coerce")))
vapply(getClass("X")@subclasses, slot, FALSE, "simple")
vapply(getClass("Y")@subclasses, slot, FALSE, "simple")
validObject(new("Z"))
```
```
> vapply(getClass("X")@subclasses, slot, FALSE, "simple")
   Y    Z 
TRUE TRUE 
> vapply(getClass("Y")@subclasses, slot, FALSE, "simple")
   Z 
TRUE 
> validObject(new("Z"))
Tracing asMethod(object) on entry 
Z->X coerce
X valid
Tracing asMethod(object) on entry 
Z->Y coerce
Y valid
Z valid
[1] TRUE
```

Whereas under patched R we see:

```
> validObject(new("Z"))
X valid
Y valid
Z valid
[1] TRUE
```

Switching to non-simple inheritance:

```
setAs("Y", "X", function (from) { to <- new("X"); to@x <- from@x; to })
setAs("Z", "X", function (from) { to <- new("X"); to@x <- from@x; to })
setAs("Z", "Y", function (from) { to <- new("Y"); to@x <- from@x;
                                                  to@y <- from@y; to })
trace("coerce", signature = c(from = "Y", to = "X"),
      tracer = quote(message("Y->X coerce")))
trace("coerce", signature = c(from = "Z", to = "X"),
      tracer = quote(message("Z->X coerce")))
trace("coerce", signature = c(from = "Z", to = "Y"),
      tracer = quote(message("Z->Y coerce")))
vapply(getClass("X")@subclasses, slot, FALSE, "simple")
vapply(getClass("Y")@subclasses, slot, FALSE, "simple")
validObject(new("Z"))
```
```
> vapply(getClass("X")@subclasses, slot, FALSE, "simple")
    Y     Z 
FALSE FALSE 
> vapply(getClass("Y")@subclasses, slot, FALSE, "simple")
    Z 
FALSE 
> validObject(new("Z"))
Tracing asMethod(object) on entry 
Z->X coerce
X valid
Tracing asMethod(object) on entry 
Z->Y coerce
Y valid
Z valid
[1] TRUE
```

Whereas under patched R we see:

```
> validObject(new("Z"))
Tracing asMethod(object) on entry 
Z->X coerce
X valid
Y valid
Z valid
[1] TRUE
```

... *missing* an expected coercion from `Z` to `Y`, revealing a bug in `setIs` that should also be fixed ...

```
> extYZ <- getClass("Y")@subclasses$Z
> extZY <- getClass("Z")@contains$Y # what validObject(new("Z")) sees
> identical(extYZ, extZY)
[1] FALSE
> extYZ@simple
[1] FALSE
> extZY@simple
[1] TRUE
```

I expect `identical(extYZ, extZY)` to be `TRUE` and `ext..@simple` to be `FALSE`.  I will want to fix that separately, as well as bug 16423.

comments.text:
> Besides introducing the cost of unnecessary coercions, it turns out that having these coercions indirectly triggers more validations than actually needed, and that these additional validations are redundant.

That is not true in general.  It is true here because your coercions call `new` with nonempty `...` and the default method for `initialize` calls `validObject` it sees nonempty `...`.  The issue is just about the extraneous coercions.
